title: File System Internals
description: Deep dive into ext4 journal modes, inode structure, directory indexing, fsync semantics, and modern file systems like XFS and ZFS.

segments.text: When your application calls write followed by close, is the data safe on disk? The answer depends on your file system, journal mode, and whether you called fsync. Getting this wrong causes silent data loss. This lesson covers the internals every database engineer needs to know.

On ext4, every file is an inode. The inode stores metadata: permissions, timestamps, size, and pointers to data blocks. A standard inode is 256 bytes. Pointers use a multi-level scheme: 12 direct pointers, one indirect, one double indirect, one triple indirect. But ext4 replaced this with extents — contiguous block ranges that reduce metadata overhead for large files.

Directories are just files containing name-to-inode mappings. Small directories use linear lists. Once a directory exceeds a block, ext4 switches to HTree indexing — essentially a B-tree hashed by filename. This is why ls on a directory with 100,000 files is fast on ext4 but painfully slow on older ext2 without indexing.

Without journaling, a crash during a write can leave the file system in an inconsistent state. Journaling writes changes to a log first, then applies them to the actual file system. If a crash occurs, the journal replays on next mount. This is why modern servers boot in seconds after a crash instead of running a full fsck.

ext4 has three journal modes. Journal mode: both data and metadata go to the journal — safest but slowest, writes data twice. Ordered mode, the default: only metadata is journaled, but data is written before metadata. Writeback mode: only metadata is journaled with no ordering guarantee — fastest but risks stale data after crash.
segments.thought_prompt: For a database that manages its own write-ahead log, which ext4 journal mode would you choose and why?

segments.text: The write syscall copies data to the kernel page cache and returns. The data is NOT on disk. Only fsync forces the kernel to flush data and metadata to persistent storage. Calling fsync is expensive — 0.5 to 5 milliseconds on SSD, 10 to 50 milliseconds on HDD. But skipping it means a power failure loses your data. Every database calls fsync after WAL writes.

fdatasync is a lighter alternative. It flushes data but skips metadata updates like access time. For appending to a log file, fdatasync saves one extra disk write per call. PostgreSQL uses fdatasync by default for WAL writes. The setting wal_sync_method controls this, and the wrong choice can halve your write throughput.

XFS excels with large files and high parallelism. It uses allocation groups — independent regions that allow concurrent allocation without global locks. This makes XFS significantly faster than ext4 for multi-threaded I/O workloads. Netflix uses XFS for their media serving infrastructure where files are multi-gigabyte and concurrent access is heavy.

ZFS takes a radically different approach with copy-on-write. Instead of modifying data in place, every write creates a new copy. This enables instant snapshots, built-in checksumming that detects bit rot, and self-healing through redundancy. The tradeoff: COW fragments files over time and requires more memory for its ARC cache.

O_DIRECT bypasses the kernel page cache entirely, reading and writing straight to disk. Databases like MySQL with InnoDB use direct I/O because they manage their own buffer pool. Double caching — once in the database buffer and once in the page cache — wastes memory. Direct I/O eliminates this but requires the application to handle its own caching.

A production database was losing committed transactions on power failure despite calling fsync. Investigation revealed the disk controller had a write cache with battery backup that had silently failed. The controller reported fsync success but data was in volatile cache. This is why distributed databases use replication — hardware lies.
segments.thought_prompt: How can you verify that fsync actually persists data to non-volatile storage on your hardware?

segments.text: File systems are the boundary between your application and persistent storage. Know your journal mode. Always fsync when durability matters. Choose ext4 for general workloads, XFS for large files with concurrent access, ZFS when you need snapshots and integrity checking. And never trust that a single disk write is durable — that's what replication is for.
